{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}
{{Short description|Competition to develop SHA-3}}
{{Use mdy dates|date = March 2019}}

The '''NIST hash function competition''' was an open competition held by the US [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] (NIST) to develop a new [[hash function]] called [[SHA-3]] to complement the older [[SHA-1]] and [[SHA-2]]. The competition was formally announced in the ''[[Federal Register]]'' on November 2, 2007.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/documents/FR_Notice_Nov07.pdf|title=Federal Register / Vol. 72, No. 212|date=November 2, 2007|access-date=2008-11-06|work=Federal Register|publisher=Government Printing Office|format=PDF}}</ref> "NIST is initiating an effort to develop one or more additional hash algorithms through a public competition, similar to the [[Advanced Encryption Standard process|development process]] for the [[Advanced Encryption Standard]] (AES)."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/index.html|title=cryptographic hash project – Background Information|access-date=2008-11-06 |work=Computer Security Resource Center|publisher=National Institute of Standards and Technology|date=November 2, 2007}}</ref> The competition ended on October 2, 2012, when NIST announced that [[Keccak]] would be the new SHA-3 hash algorithm.<ref name="NIST">{{cite web|url=https://www.nist.gov/itl/csd/sha-100212.cfm|title=NIST Selects Winner of Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA-3) Competition|publisher=NIST|date=October 2, 2012|access-date=October 2, 2012}}</ref>

The winning hash function has been published as NIST FIPS 202 the "SHA-3 Standard", to complement FIPS 180-4, the ''[[Secure Hash Standard]]''.

The NIST competition has inspired other competitions such as the [[Password Hashing Competition]].

==Process==
Submissions were due October 31, 2008 and the list of candidates accepted for the first round was published on December 9, 2008.<ref name="Round1">{{cite web|url=http://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/sha-3/Round1/index.html|title=Round 1|date=2008-12-09|access-date=2008-12-10}}</ref> NIST held a conference in late February 2009 where submitters presented their algorithms and NIST officials discussed criteria for narrowing down the field of candidates for Round 2.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/sha-3/Round1/Feb2009/index.html|title=The First SHA-3 Candidate Conference|author=National Institute of Standards and Technology|date=December 9, 2008|access-date=23 December 2008}}</ref> The list of 14 candidates accepted to Round 2 was published on July 24, 2009.<ref name="Round2">{{cite web|url=http://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/sha-3/Round2/submissions_rnd2.html|title=Second Round Candidates|publisher=National Institute for Standards and Technology|date=July 24, 2009|access-date=July 24, 2009}}</ref> Another conference was held on August 23–24, 2010 (after [[International Cryptology Conference|CRYPTO]] 2010) at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]], where the second-round candidates were discussed.<ref name="conference2">{{cite web|url=https://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/sha-3/Round2/Aug2010/|title=The Second SHA-3 Candidate Conference|author=National Institute of Standards and Technology|date=June 30, 2010}}</ref> The announcement of the final round candidates occurred on December 10, 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/timeline.html|title=Tentative Timeline of the Development of New Hash Functions|publisher=NIST|date=December 10, 2008|access-date=September 15, 2009}}</ref> On October 2, 2012, NIST announced its winner, choosing [[Keccak]], created by Guido Bertoni, Joan Daemen, and Gilles Van Assche of STMicroelectronics and Michaël Peeters of NXP.<ref name="NIST"/>

==Entrants==
This is an incomplete list of known submissions.
NIST selected 51 entries for round 1.<ref name="Round1" /> 14 of them advanced to round 2,<ref name="Round2" /> from which 5 finalists were selected.

===Winner===
The winner was announced to be [[Keccak]] on October 2, 2012.<ref>[https://www.nist.gov/itl/csd/sha-100212.cfm NIST Selects Winner of Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA-3) Competition]</ref>

===Finalists===
NIST selected five SHA-3 candidate algorithms to advance to the third (and final) round:<ref>[http://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/sha-3/Round3/submissions_rnd3.html Third (Final) Round Candidates] Retrieved 9 Nov 2011</ref>
*[[BLAKE (hash function)|BLAKE]] (Aumasson et al.)
*[[Grøstl]] ([[Lars Ramkilde Knudsen|Knudsen]] et al.)
*[[JH (hash function)|JH]] (Hongjun Wu)
*[[Keccak]] (Keccak team, [[Joan Daemen|Daemen]] et al.)
*[[Skein (hash function)|Skein]] ([[Bruce Schneier|Schneier]] et al.)

NIST noted some factors that figured into its selection as it announced the finalists:<ref>[http://crypto.junod.info/2010/12/10/sha-3-finalists-announced-by-nist/ SHA-3 Finalists Announced by NIST] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110709093032/http://crypto.junod.info/2010/12/10/sha-3-finalists-announced-by-nist/ |date=July 9, 2011 }}, blog post quoting NIST's announcement in full.</ref>

*Performance: "A couple of algorithms were wounded or eliminated by very large [hardware gate] area requirement – it seemed that the area they required precluded their use in too much of the potential application space."
*Security: "We preferred to be conservative about security, and in some cases did not select algorithms with exceptional performance, largely because something about them made us 'nervous,' even though we knew of no clear attack against the full algorithm."
*Analysis: "NIST eliminated several algorithms because of the extent of their second-round tweaks or because of a relative lack of reported [[cryptanalysis]] – either tended to create the suspicion that the design might not yet be fully tested and mature."
*Diversity: The finalists included hashes based on different modes of operation, including the HAIFA and [[sponge function]] constructions, and with different internal structures, including ones based on AES, bitslicing, and alternating XOR with addition.

NIST has released a report explaining its evaluation algorithm-by-algorithm.<ref>[http://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/sha-3/Round1/documents/sha3_NISTIR7620.pdf Status Report on the first round of the SHA-3 Cryptographic Hash Algorithm Competition] (PDF).</ref><ref>[http://csrc.nist.gov/groups/ST/hash/sha-3/Round2/documents/Round2_Report_NISTIR_7764.pdf Status Report on the second round of the SHA-3 Cryptographic Hash Algorithm Competition] (PDF). Retrieved 2 March 2011</ref><ref>[https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2012/NIST.IR.7896.pdf Third-Round Report of the SHA-3 Cryptographic Hash Algorithm Competition] (PDF).</ref>

===Rejected entrants===
Several submissions received by NIST were not accepted as first-round candidates, following an internal review by NIST.<ref name="Round1" /> In general, NIST gave no details as to why each was rejected. NIST also has not given a comprehensive list of rejected algorithms; there are known to be 13,<ref name="Round1" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2008/11/skein_and_sha-3.html|title=Skein and SHA-3 News|author=Bruce Schneier|date=November 19, 2008|access-date=23 December 2008}}</ref> but only the following are public.

{{div col|colwidth=22em}}
*HASH 2X{{Citation needed|date=May 2018}}
*Maraca<ref>{{cite web|url=http://burtleburtle.net/bob/crypto/maraca/nist/|title=Algorithm Specification|author=Robert J. Jenkins Jr.|access-date=15 December 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://ehash.iaik.tugraz.at/uploads/5/52/Maraca.pdf|title=Internal collision attack on Maraca|format=PDF|author=Anne Canteaut|author2=María Naya-Plasencia|name-list-style=amp|access-date=15 December 2008}}</ref>
*MIXIT<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/3133557/Bitcoin/mixit-spec.pdf|title=Algorithm Specification for MIXIT: a SHA-3 Candidate Cryptographic Hash Algorithm|author=Michael P. Frank|access-date=12 January 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304051325/https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/3133557/Bitcoin/mixit-spec.pdf|archive-date=March 4, 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>
*NKS 2D<ref>{{cite web|url=http://geoffrey.park.googlepages.com/SHA3Submission01.pdf|title=NKS 2D Cellular Automata Hash|access-date=2008-11-09|author=Geoffrey Park|format=PDF}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://ehash.iaik.tugraz.at/uploads/3/3f/NK2SD-224.txt|title=Collisions for NKS2D-224|author=Cristophe De Cannière|access-date=14 November 2008|date=November 13, 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://ehash.iaik.tugraz.at/uploads/9/93/NK2SD-512.txt|title=Collisions for NKS2D-512|author=Brandon Enright|access-date=14 November 2008|date=November 14, 2008}}</ref>
*Ponic<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ehash.iaik.tugraz.at/uploads/3/3c/PonicSpecification.pdf|title=Ponic|access-date=2008-11-09|author=Peter Schmidt-Nielsen|format=PDF}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://131002.net/data/papers/ponic.pdf|title=Second preimage attack on Ponic|format=PDF|author=María Naya-Plasencia|access-date=30 November 2008}}</ref>
*ZK-Crypt<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fortressgb.com/apage/39649.php|title=ZK-Crypt Homepage|author=Nicolas T. Courtois|author2=Carmi Gressel|author3=Avi Hecht|author4=Gregory V. Bard|author5=Ran Granot|access-date=1 March 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090209040334/http://fortressgb.com/apage/39649.php|archive-date=9 February 2009}}</ref>
